Ansel Adams. An American landscape and environmental photographer renowned for his dramatic black-and-white photographs of the American West, particularly Yosemite National Park. He developed the Zone System, a sophisticated method for metering light and controlling exposure and printing tone, and became an evangelist for photography as a fine art equal to painting and sculpture.

Adams pioneered the Zone System, a methodology for translating a scene's tonal range into a final print through careful metering, exposure, and darkroom technique. This system is still taught to photographers today. He created iconic images of El Capitan, Half Dome, and Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico. These monumental landscapes conveyed wilderness majesty and environmental fragility at a time before environmentalism became mainstream.

In 1932 Adams founded the Group f/64, a collective of photographers advocating for sharp focus, rich tonal detail, and fine prints. This was a deliberate rejection of pictorialism and a defence of photography's unique aesthetic. He wrote seminal technical texts: The Negative, The Print, and The Camera. These treatises on craft remain authoritative and accessible to both amateurs and professionals. Beyond his work in the darkroom, Adams also served as a conservationist, using his photographs to advocate for wilderness preservation, particularly in California's Sierra Nevada.

Adams built on the foundation laid by Alfred Stieglitz, the earlier fine-art photographer whose championing of photography's artistic legitimacy paved the way for his own career and philosophy. He inherited his systematic approach to exposure and printing from Eadweard Muybridge's rigorous technical control of photography. His meditative landscape approach contrasted with Henri Cartier-Bresson's street photography aesthetic, yet both photographers shared ambitious artistic goals.
